issues.issue: The provision is hortatory ("share the responsibility", "requires the cooperation of all") and states no rule capable of application, so its operative content is uncertain.

The prohibited behaviors are single undefined words — "intimidates", "harasses or bullies", "invades personal privacy", "endangers the health, safety, or welfare" — each of which is reasonably susceptible to broad and narrow readings when applied to particular conduct.

2.1.f permits campus restriction or emergency suspension merely because a student is "involved in such an incident", whereas Section 22.2 forbids altering a student's status pending final action "except for reasons of imminent danger".
"Comply with instructions of University officials" sets no limit on which instructions bind a student, so its reach cannot be measured from the text.

"[O]r other authorized functions" is a catch-all appended to the enumerated teaching, research, administrative, public service and disciplinary functions, leaving its reach open to ejusdem generis argument.
"[C]auses disruption to or invades another individual's privacy" is undefined and "other electronic devices" is an open catch-all after a specific list of devices.
"[I]ssuing any type of threat is strictly prohibited" is an unbounded prohibition dropped into a provision about safety equipment, and "only when it is necessary" supplies no standard of necessity.

The protected categories listed here are a closed list, while Section 7.0 lists a partly different set and adds "any other category protected by law", so the two statements of the same prohibition do not match.

The hazing definition turns on "humiliates, degrades, abuses, or endangers" and lists examples such as "alcohol consumption" and "isolation" that are innocuous in themselves, leaving the boundary of the offense uncertain.

"[A]nd other articles or substances usable as weapons" is a general catch-all following an enumerated list of firearms, explosives, knives and fireworks, and almost any object is "usable as" a weapon.

The first sentence bars bringing "any dog or animal onto the campus without a leash" while the second sentence carves out guide and service animals only from the building restriction, leaving the exception's scope unclear.
"Assume responsibility for the actions, damage, or injuries caused by" a guest is an open-ended liability with no stated limit or causation standard.

The provision incorporates "regulations enumerated in other official University publications and documents" by an "e.g." list, so which outside documents are made binding cannot be determined from the text.
"[A]ny verbal or physical behavior or actions that could be construed as retaliation" makes the offense turn on a possible construction by an unnamed observer rather than on any objective standard.

The section mixes exhortation ("students are encouraged to examine their own values") with the operative statement that non-consensual interaction "could be defined as sexual misconduct", and neither "sexual misconduct" nor the required affirmative seeking of consent is defined.

It permits emergency suspension of "any student accused of sexual misconduct" pending investigation, which cannot be squared with Section 22.2's rule that status shall not be altered pending final action except for "imminent danger".

"Sexual contact that occurs without the explicit consent of each person involved may be considered sexual misconduct" uses permissive "may be considered", so the text does not say when non-consensual contact is a violation.
The requirement of "explicit consent" that is "clearly and affirmatively communicated" cannot be reconciled with Section 3.3, which says consent "may be communicated verbally or through actions".

"[T]aking advantage of someone's incapacitation or intoxication" is undefined and, unlike Section 3.1, uses "intoxication" as an alternative to incapacity without saying what degree of intoxication suffices.
"[A]dvantage gained by the Accuser's mental or physical incapacity ... of which the Accused was aware or should have been aware" imposes a constructive-knowledge test with no stated benchmark.
Allowing consent to be communicated "through actions" conflicts with Section 3.1's requirement of "explicit consent" that is "clearly and affirmatively communicated".
"[P]assive assistance of legal counsel" is undefined, so what an attorney may actually do for a party in the Special Examiner's Process cannot be determined from the words.

This summary says Section 22.6 merely "permits the passive assistance of legal counsel", while the Advisor definition in Section 22.6 says the Advisor role itself "may instead be held by a party's attorney" when criminal proceedings coexist.
"[I]nsofar as they relate to the Accuser" gives no way to tell which parts of an outcome must be disclosed.
"[A]ny reasonably available changes in academic or living situations" is an undefined obligation with no measure of what is reasonably available.
The Department may remove chalked messages that are "inappropriate or use profane illustrations or language", a standard with no defined boundary.
"[O]r in appropriate use of property" is a mechanical error: the split word reads as its own opposite, and only context suggests "inappropriate" was meant.
"Mistreatment of animals, trees, or plantings" is undefined and its boundary against ordinary use of the grounds cannot be drawn from the text.

The protected-class list is garbled ("Vietnam Era Veteran, qualified special, disabled veteran") and closes with the catch-all "any other category protected by law", so both the list's content and its reach are uncertain.

The section makes any Section 7 allegation adjudicable under the Special Examiner's Process, but Section 7 itself never defines the prohibited conduct that the Special Examiner is to find, leaving it dependent on Sections 7.1–7.3's examples.

Harassment is defined by its "purpose or effect of unreasonably interfering" and creation of an "intimidating, hostile or offensive environment", standards whose application to particular conduct is contestable on the face of the words.
The protected-class list here says "gender" while Section 7.0 says "gender identity and expression" and Section 7.3 says "gender expression", so the same policy states three different lists.

The enumerated examples are prefaced by "includes, but is not limited to" and qualified by "[d]epending on the circumstances", so whether unlisted conduct is sexual harassment cannot be resolved from the list.

The list is expressly "not an exhaustive list" and closes with the catch-all "[o]ther verbal or physical conduct that denigrates or shows hostility", so the general term's reach against the specifics is open.

The closing sentence that the University "may take action on conduct that it deems to be inappropriate, regardless of whether it rises to the level of a violation of law" sits awkwardly with the enumerated standards that purport to define what is prohibited.
"[F]alsified a claim" is not defined and does not distinguish a knowingly false report from an unsubstantiated one.
"[O]r other non-University related purposes" is a general catch-all after "commercial, political", leaving unclear how far beyond those specifics it reaches.
The 1947 recital about the change of the University's name points nowhere in the operative permission that follows, which concerns only recognized student organizations' use of the name.

"The privacy of every individual in person and in their room and/or office must be respected" states an undefined duty of respect whose scope, unlike the specific entry prohibition that follows, cannot be drawn from the words.

Routine inspections "to check for illegal possession of University-owned property" on 24 hours' public notice are hard to square with Section 17.2, which requires advance written permission from the Senior Student Affairs Officer for entry to search a student-maintained room and excepts only Section 10.5.
The gatekeeping standards — reports "in a timely manner", cases that "lack[] merit", and matters "not reported in a timely fashion" — supply no measure of timeliness or merit.

The statement that disciplinary action "may be implemented only through the report of a violation to the DSRCS" cannot be reconciled with Section 22.6, which lets the SSAO/D act where there is no Accuser, and with Sections 22.1–22.4, which authorize University Actions without any report.

The mediated outcome is described as "agreed-upon, recorded, final, and binding" while the same process is "informal, non-adversarial" and subject to the Director's approval, leaving the finality of the outcome uncertain.

The description of the outcome as "final, and binding" is difficult to square with Section 18.2, which allows the Director to declare an endpoint and redirect the matter into the Section 19 conduct process.
A parenthesis opened after "the appropriate administrator (" swallows the operative deemed-admission rule and the deferral note, so the punctuation leaves the status of the enclosed text uncertain.

The provision directs the administrator to "proceed to sanctioning in accordance with Section 19.3", but Section 19.3 addresses only failure to attend a meeting after choosing Administrative Action and prescribes no sanctioning procedure.

"An Accused's failure to choose one of the options within 2 business days constitutes an acceptance of responsibility" deems an admission from silence, and "extenuating circumstances" is left undefined.
It again routes the administrator to "sanctioning in accordance with Section 19.3", which contains no sanctioning procedure and deals only with missed Administrative Action meetings.

"[U]nder the Administrative Action option, this is the only opportunity to present evidence" sits oddly with the same sentence's provision that the meeting may be "waived in the event of" the Preliminary Meeting, leaving the accused's evidentiary opportunity unclear.

Sections 19.1, 19.6.k and 19.7 all treat Section 19.3 as the route to sanctioning after a deemed acceptance of responsibility, but this provision describes only completion of an Administrative Action meeting in the student's absence.
"Pending charges may be discontinued thereafter dependent upon the conduct of the Accused" gives no standard for discontinuance and does not say what happens if the 90-day cap is reached.

Deferral for a student's withdrawal cannot be squared with the Special Examiner's Process, which provides that once activated by a CSR it "may not be interrupted by the withdrawal from the University by the Accused".
"[W]ithin 30 class days, or as soon as practicable" makes the deadline self-cancelling, since the alternative has no fixed limit.

It lets "the Accused and Accuser" agree to proceed without the prescribed minimum voting composition, while Section 20.2 requires that waiver to be by mutual consent of the SCB as well as the two parties.

The Advisor's role is "passive assistance", yet the same provision allows the Hearing Administrator to permit "active participation ... [i]n exceptional circumstances", and neither term nor the exception is defined.

It bars retaining "professional legal counsel or other persons from outside the University community" to advise the student, whereas the Advisor definition in Section 22.6 allows the Advisor role itself to be held by a party's attorney when criminal proceedings coexist.
The parenthesis in "(except as provided in Section 19.6.k." is never closed, and Section 19.6.k in fact provides no exception permitting a party's absence, only rescheduling and a deemed acceptance.

The provision guarantees the right "to question all witnesses appearing before the Board and only at the hearing" yet in the next breath allows the Board to receive written testimony from absentee witnesses, which cannot be questioned.

"[T]he burden of proof shall rest upon the Accuser" does not say what standard the Accuser must meet, and Section 18.0 contemplates that the Accuser may be a "reporting agency" rather than a person able to carry a burden.

No corresponding burden is allocated in the Special Examiner's Process of Section 22.6, where the Special Examiner both investigates and makes the responsibility finding, so identical charges carry different burdens depending on the route.

A finding of responsibility here requires "clear and convincing evidence", while the Standard of Evaluation in Section 22.6 applies a "preponderance of the evidence" to the same student code, leaving the code with two inconsistent standards of proof.

Failure to attend at one's own "fault", as determined by the Hearing Administrator, is deemed an acceptance of responsibility, but "fault" is undefined and the deemed admission follows from mere non-attendance.
Section 19.6.e treats this provision as supplying an exception to the requirement that the parties be present, but 19.6.k contains no such exception.

The appeal grounds are exclusive ("based only on") yet include "denial of rights under this process" and "procedural error", which are undefined and potentially open-ended against the specific grounds of fraud and new evidence.

It provides that the UAB "shall conduct a new hearing" and that sanctions "shall not take effect until approved or modified", which cannot be squared with the Section 22.6 appeal, where the UAB only reports opinions and sanctions take effect immediately regardless of appeal.

The listed "Rights to Fairness" include a right "[t]o remain silent and not testify against themselves" immediately qualified by the warning that the Board will decide on the evidence presented, leaving the content of the right uncertain.

These rights are stated to apply "under this process", yet the Special Examiner's Process of Section 22.6 — which governs all Section 3 and Section 7 charges — affords none of them, so the instrument promises fairness rights that its own principal disciplinary track withholds.
A not-responsible outcome is nonetheless "pending approval by the Senior Student Affairs Officer or designee", which leaves unclear whether an acquittal by the Board is final.

Starting a Sanction Hearing at step O "after introductory remarks in A. and B." skips step C, in which the Chairperson reads the parties' Rights to Fairness, so a student accepting responsibility is never read those rights.

The required voting panels (four voters) sit uneasily with Section 19.6.i's rule that the Chairperson votes only to break a tie, since the text does not say whether the student Chairperson is one of the required voters.

Waiver here requires "mutual consent of the SCB, the Accuser, and the Accused", whereas Section 19.6.c allows the Accused and Accuser alone to agree to proceed without the prescribed minimum voting composition.
"Staff members appointed by the Senior Student Affairs Officer or designee" is a sentence without a verb, leaving the appointment mechanism stated only by implication.
"[O]f a representative cross-section of Brandeis students, as allowed by those who apply" is garbled and self-cancelling as a composition requirement.
The parenthesis in "designee see Section 19.8 for information on Administrative Action review)" is unopened, obscuring whether the cross-reference qualifies the UAB's appellate jurisdiction.

It provides that "[a]n administrator from the Division of Students and Enrollment ... will serve as Chairperson of the University Appeals Board", while Section 20.8 requires a Chairperson who is a full-time tenured faculty member.
The provision requires "one tenured faculty Chairperson" appointed by the SSAO/D but also refers to a term of appointment "for faculty and staff members" although no staff serve on the UAB.

The composition stated here (one full-time student and two faculty, chaired by tenured faculty) conflicts with Section 20.7's administrator-Chairperson and with the Section 22.6 definition of the UAB as "faculty membership only".

The sanctioning factors are "including but not limited to" an enumerated list, and the learning-component requirement applies only "whenever appropriate", giving the general terms no measurable boundary.

"Sanctions shall not take effect until approved" and "[s]uspensions or dismissals shall not take effect until approved by the SSAO/D" cannot be squared with Section 22.6's rule that "[a]ny and all sanctions, including suspension or dismissal, will be in effect immediately, regardless of any appeal".
"[C]ertain University privileges including, but not limited to" an enumerated list leaves the catch-all's reach — which privileges may be withdrawn — undetermined.
Probation may be revoked if the student "in any way fail[s] to conduct themselves as a responsible member of the University community", a standard with no ascertainable content.

The sentence "Suspension may extend for a semester, until a designated date, and/or until degrees/certificates will not be issued and credit will not be granted for courses taken elsewhere" is broken — text is plainly missing after "until" — so the duration rule cannot be read as written.

"[T]he University may take any action that it believes to be appropriate and reasonable", closing with "or other action deemed necessary", is a self-judging catch-all whose limits cannot be derived from the enumerated examples.

The unlimited power to act whenever conduct "may disrupt the safety or well-being" of another cannot be reconciled with Section 22.2, which forbids altering a student's status pending final action except for "imminent danger".
"[I]mminent danger to their physical or emotional safety or well-being" is an undefined and elastic trigger for separating a student from campus.

The rule that status "shall not be altered" except for imminent danger conflicts with Sections 2.1.f and 3.0, which permit emergency suspension of any student merely accused pending investigation, and with Section 22.1's power to take "any action" it believes appropriate.
"[C]harged with or convicted of a crime" is unlimited as to the kind or seriousness of the offense, and the SSAO/D's obligation to "consider the nature of the crime" supplies no standard.

Its statement that "[t]he procedural standards set forth in Section 19 do not apply" cannot be squared with Section 22.2, which requires the Section 19.1 procedures to be implemented within 10 class days of any separation from campus.

Discipline turns on off-campus behavior that "in the judgment of the [SSAO/D]" is inconsistent with being a "good citizen[] and good neighbor[]" and "adversely affects the University community" — a wholly subjective and unbounded standard.

The exclusion of Section 19's procedural standards from "off-campus behavior" is inconsistent with Section 2.1.f, which makes conduct endangering others "on or off campus" a code violation adjudicated through the conduct process.
"[S]evere emotional or psychological distress" and the undefined "emergency protocol" leave both the trigger and the content of the University's action unstated.

A blanket exclusion from campus with "no exception for examinations" until written permission is given sits uneasily with Section 22.5's own promise of a contest opportunity within 3 business days and with Section 22.2's imminent-danger limit on altering a student's status.

The reservation of a right to act where there is "no Accuser" under Section 22.1 authority cannot be squared with Section 18.0, which says disciplinary action "may be implemented only through the report of a violation to the DSRCS" by an Accuser.

"[E]xcept when co-existing criminal proceedings exist, in which case the Advisor role may instead be held by a party's attorney" leaves unclear whose option "may" is and what an attorney-Advisor may do, given the role is "passive"; the sentence "and Advisor is not required" is also mistyped.

Allowing an attorney to hold the Advisor role conflicts with Section 19.6.d, which bars "persons from outside the University community" from advising a student and allows only "passive assistance of legal counsel" when criminal charges coexist.
The report is said to be submitted "in support of the Responsibility Findings and/or Deliberations Phase", and "and/or" leaves the report's function in each phase indeterminate.

This definition makes the Special Examiner the finder of responsibility, while the SSAO/D definition makes the SSAO/D responsible for "rendering the final decision" and the Appeals Procedures speak of "the final decision by the panel".

The definition ("present during the alleged incident(s) or who has direct knowledge") differs from Section 19.6.e's definition of witnesses as those present "and/or [who] have information directly related to the incident".
The SSAO/D is said to render "the final decision as to any outcome", which cannot be squared with the Appeals Procedures' reference to appealing "the final decision by the panel".
The panel is defined as making only "a recommendation to the SSAO/D", yet the Appeals Procedures describe an appeal from "the final decision by the panel".

Defining the UAB as "faculty membership only" contradicts Section 20.8, which requires one full-time student among the three voting members, and Section 20.7, which gives the UAB an administrator Chairperson.
The preponderance standard adopted here conflicts with Section 19.6.i, under which a finding of responsibility on the same student code may be made "based only upon clear and convincing evidence".

"[C]onducted deliberately and without unnecessary delay" and a 60-day "goal ... or as soon as is practicable if unusual circumstances exist" state an aspiration rather than a deadline, leaving whether any time limit binds the University open.

"If the Accused fails to cooperate prior to accepting or denying responsibility ... the Director or the Special Examiner may consider the Accused to have accepted responsibility" turns an undefined failure to "cooperate" into an admission of guilt.

The statement that the process "may not be interrupted by the withdrawal from the University by the Accused" conflicts with Sections 19.1 and 19.4, which allow deferral of conduct proceedings on a student's withdrawal.

The duty to log and share evidence extends only to what the Special Examiner "deem[s] ... to be of material importance", and the reserved "discretion not to share certain records due to confidentiality concerns" leaves the exception potentially wider than the rule.

The promise to share evidence "equally with the parties to ensure the opportunity for response" is difficult to reconcile with Section 19.6.g's guarantee that the parties may "view and question all evidence and reports presented", since here disclosure is discretionary.
Whether anyone is interviewed at all is left "at the discretion of the Special Examiner", with no standard governing that discretion.

The Observer's role is "passive, with the exception of providing supplemental description of details regarding procedures and University services", which is a self-contradictory description of passivity.
"[G]ood-faith effort to contact all pertinent witnesses" gives no benchmark for either good faith or pertinence, and the Special Examiner alone decides who is interviewed.
The report "makes a finding about whether the Accused is responsible", but the text does not say whether that finding is itself the adjudication or merely a recommendation.

Making the Special Examiner the finder of responsibility cannot be squared with the SSAO/D definition, which makes the SSAO/D responsible for "rendering the final decision", or with the Appeals Procedures' "final decision by the panel".

The parties are given only the SSAO/D's oral "summary of findings" to respond to, which is hard to reconcile with the Documents provision's promise that materially important evidence "will be logged and shared equally with the parties to ensure the opportunity for response".
The provision says only that the Accused "is found" responsible or not responsible, without stating who makes that finding.

Read with the Special Examiner and Panel definitions, it leaves the responsibility finding attributed to the Special Examiner while the SSAO/D is said to render the final decision, an allocation the instrument never reconciles.
The panel is said to "make recommendations as to the outcome(s)", which cannot be squared with the Appeals Procedures' description of an appeal from "the final decision by the panel".
"Upon voting, the panel will communicate its recommendations" describes an advisory vote, in tension with the Appeals Procedures, which treat the panel as having made a "final decision".
"The SSAO/D will render the final decision as to any outcomes" directly contradicts the Appeals Procedures, which give the parties a right to appeal "the final decision by the panel".
"[A]ny sanctions that relate to them in accordance with applicable laws" leaves both which sanctions relate to the Accuser and which laws govern disclosure unstated.

Immediate effect "regardless of any appeal" contradicts Section 21.1 ("Sanctions shall not take effect until approved"; suspensions and dismissals not until approved by the SSAO/D) and Section 19.7 (sanctions not effective until approved or modified after appeal).

The right to appeal "the final decision by the panel" cannot be reconciled with the Panel definition and Deliberations Phase, under which the panel only recommends, and with the statement that "[t]he SSAO/D will render the final decision as to any outcomes".

Barring appeals grounded in "dissatisfaction with an imposed sanction" is hard to square with the appeal right granted over the panel's outcome decision, which is the sanction itself, and with the UAB's charge to address "the specific concerns of the Appellant".
